endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Conduct and document an AI System Impact Assessment that includes evaluation of risks and benefits for AI solutions.

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Patel and Blumenthal14 argue that GenAI is too broad, adaptive, and opaque to be evaluated effectively through current medical device regulatory frameworks and instead propose competency-based regulation modeled on medical training, licensure examinations, supervised practice, periodic reevaluation, and public reporting.

endorsements.title: Agentic AI in radiology: emerging potential and unresolved challenges
endorsements.quote: Radiologists must maintain ultimate oversight and decision-making authority, but institutions will need clear policies defining the acceptable boundaries of AI-initiated actions.

endorsements.title: Generative AI as interactional infrastructure for meaning-centered care in later life
endorsements.quote: Fully automated routing, triage, or service allocation for emotionally or clinically complex concerns.

endorsements.title: Medical AI Agents for Clinical Decision Support: Viewpoint Using the Planning, Action, Reflection, and Memory (PARM) Analytical Lens
endorsements.quote: Boundaries must be specified across multiple dimensions: clinical scope (eg, which situations and which patient populations), authority to act (eg, information retrieval and order entry), and decision risk (eg, routine monitoring and critical interventions).

endorsements.title: Promise, Mimicry, and Surveillance: Responsibly Integrating Artificial Intelligence With Socratic Inquiry in Medical Education
endorsements.quote: Autonomous use, in which AI determines judgments without human oversight, is the highest-risk category and should be avoided.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether documenting and bounding agentic AI autonomy prevents unauthorized, irreversible, or scope-creeping actions, and no study documents how often such actions occur. Six sources endorse the practice, and all of them rest on expert reasoning rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and zero studies of the hazard. The six endorsements include one framework, one regulatory discussion paper, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures the frequency or severity of harmful actions taken by AI agents across connected clinical systems. Without a hazard study, deployers cannot yet tell whether human checkpoints and reversibility requirements would catch errors before they reach patients, or which action types carry the most risk.

The regulatory discussion paper describes a proposal for competency-based oversight modeled on supervised practice and periodic reevaluation, which differs from current device review. This source describes a proposal rather than an adopted rule. Deployers therefore face no identified federal requirement specific to agent autonomy bounds among the supplied sources.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should record the actions AI agents take in live clinical and administrative systems, count unauthorized or irreversible actions, and compare deployments with and without documented autonomy bounds, human checkpoints, and vendor disclosure.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence addresses Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups cannot draw on data showing whether autonomy bounds protect their patients, including those whose concerns one commentary flags as unsuitable for fully automated routing or triage.
